claim: Five fruit fly models of familial Parkinsonism were developed carrying pathogenic mutations in lrrk, rab39, auxilin (aux), synaptojanin (synj), and pink1 genes.
source: We selected homologues of five PD genes and replaced the Drosophila lrrk, rab39, auxilin (aux), synaptojanin (synj), and pink1 genes by wild-type and pathogenic mutant human or Drosophila coding DNA (cDNA) sequences (CDS) at the endogenous locus (Figure 1a; wild-type hPINK1 was a UAS construct; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the generation of five fly models with specific gene replacements at endogenous loci.

claim: The wild-type and pathogenic mutant human or Drosophila coding sequences are expressed at endogenous levels in the knock-in models.
source: We confirm that the wild-type and pathogenic mutant human CDS (LRRK2, RAB39B, and PINK1) or Drosophila CDS (DNAJC6 (Aux) and SYNJ1 (Synj)) are expressed at endogenous levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Expression levels were confirmed through RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: PD knock-in models show disturbances in mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: For example, we find disturbances in mitochondrial membrane potential and electrophysiological defects in electroretinogram (ERG) recordings of flies stressed by exposure to constant light for 7 days (Hindle et al., 2013; Morais et al., 2009; Mortiboys et al., 2010; Ng et al., 2012; Vanhauwaert et al., 2017; Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: Mitochondrial membrane potential was measured using TMRE fluorescence at neuromuscular junction boutons, as shown in Figure 1b.

claim: PD knock-in models show electrophysiological defects in electroretinogram recordings after exposure to constant light for 7 days.
source: For example, we find disturbances in mitochondrial membrane potential and electrophysiological defects in electroretinogram (ERG) recordings of flies stressed by exposure to constant light for 7 days (Hindle et al., 2013; Morais et al., 2009; Mortiboys et al., 2010; Ng et al., 2012; Vanhauwaert et al., 2017; Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: ERG recordings were performed after 7 days of light exposure, with results shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Young PD knock-in flies (5 days old) do not show defects in startle-induced negative geotaxis (SING) assay.
source: Similarly, none of our models shows a SING defect at a young age (5 days, young) (Figure 1b).
evidence: SING performance was quantified in 5-day-old flies and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Old PD knock-in flies (25 days old) display impaired performance in the SING assay.
source: However, as flies get older (25 days, old), the PD knock-ins display impaired performance in this DAN-dependent locomotion assay, while the performance of controls is not affected (Figure 1b).
evidence: SING performance was quantified in 25-day-old flies and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: SING defects in PD mutant models are rescued when flies are fed L-DOPA but not D-DOPA.
source: This is in line with recent work where we show that SING defects in PD mutant models are rescued when the flies are fed L-DOPA but not D-DOPA, indicating a very strong correlation between SING defects and defects in dopaminergic synaptic innervation of PAM DAN onto mushroom body neurons (Kaempf et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent work (Kaempf et al., 2024).

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing was conducted on entire brains of young (5-day-old) animals from five PD mutants and controls.
source: To define cell types affected by pathogenic PD mutations early in life, we used an unbiased approach and conducted single-cell RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of entire brains of young (5 days) animals (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes conducting single-cell RNA sequencing on young fly brains.

claim: 108,000 newly sequenced cells from five mutants and controls were pooled with 118,000 wild-type cells from the original atlas, leading to 186 cell clusters.
source: We pooled 108k newly sequenced cells from these five mutants and controls with the 118k wild-type cells from our original atlas leading to 186 cell clusters, of which 81 were annotated to known cell types (Davie et al., 2018; Janssens et al., 2022; Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific cell counts and cluster numbers, with visualization in Figure 2a.

claim: PD mutant cells equally mix with cells of the original fly brain cell atlas.
source: PD mutant cells equally mix with the cells of the original fly brain cell atlas, and the frequency of recovered cell types is similar between control and mutant brains (including DAN; Figure 2b–f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The mixing of cells is shown in Figures 2b-f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: The frequency of recovered cell types is similar between control and mutant brains.
source: PD mutant cells equally mix with the cells of the original fly brain cell atlas, and the frequency of recovered cell types is similar between control and mutant brains (including DAN; Figure 2b–f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Cell type frequencies are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: No cell type shows higher or lower expression of the knocked-in coding sequences.
source: We further do not find any cell type that shows higher or lower expression of the knocked-in CDS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Expression levels across cell types are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Cellular identity and cellular composition are preserved in young PD fly models.
source: Thus, cellular identity and cellular composition are preserved in young PD fly models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that cell type frequencies and mixing are similar between mutants and controls.

claim: Eight common predominantly affected cell types were found across the five mutants.
source: Using the residuals of this model we find eight common predominantly affected cell types across the five mutants (Supplementary file 5 and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The manuscript describes using a negative binomial model to identify affected cell types.

claim: Commonly affected cell types include cholinergic olfactory projection neurons (OPNs), Kenyon cells, cholinergic neurons of the visual system (T1 neurons), and other yet-to-be-identified cell types.
source: The commonly affected cell types include cholinergic olfactory projection neurons (OPNs), Kenyon cells, cholinergic neurons of the visual system (T1 neurons), and other yet-to-be-identified cell types (Figure 2b–f, black cells; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Affected cell types are shown as black cells in Figures 2b-f.

claim: Glial subtypes were affected in PINK1P399L mutants.
source: We also find cell types uniquely affected in some mutants, e.g., glial subtypes that were affected in PINK1P399L.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that glial subtypes were affected in PINK1P399L mutants.

claim: Olfactory projection neurons are higher-order projection neurons that control innate olfactory processing and odor classification.
source: While several cell types are affected (and many are cholinergic), OPN are here of particular interest because they are higher-order projection neurons that control innate olfactory processing and odor classification (Masse et al., 2009).
evidence: The function of OPNs is supported by a citation to Masse et al., 2009.

claim: Single nucleus sequencing was performed on nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM), nucleus accumbens, and putamen from five brains of PD patients and five brains from unaffected age-matched individuals.
source: We analyzed nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM), nucleus accumbens, and putamen from five brains of PD patients (all have idiopathic LRRK2 risk mutations) and five brains from unaffected age-matched individuals (without PD-relevant genetic variants).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the human brain samples analyzed.

claim: 37 distinct cell types were identified in the human brain samples.
source: Our analysis identified 37 distinct cell types in these brain regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), and most of the cell types have a similar frequency when comparing PD versus non-PD condition.
evidence: Cell types are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A microglia subtype (MG #20) shows a 900% increase in frequency in PD patient brains compared to non-PD samples.
source: An exception is a microglia subtype (MG #20, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b), which is 900% increase in frequency in PD patient brains compared to non-PD samples.
evidence: The frequency increase is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Many differentially expressed genes in human brain samples are genes encoding synaptic proteins listed in the synapse-specific portal SynGo.
source: Many of the DEG are genes encoding synaptic proteins that are also listed in the synapse-specific portal SynGo (Koopmans et al., 2019; Figure 3a and a'; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The overlap with SynGo is shown in Figure 3a and a'.

claim: More than 20% of the neuronal differentially expressed genes in nucleus basalis of Meynert that have an orthologous gene in the fly are also found among the most deregulated genes across PD fly models.
source: For example, in the NBM, an area associated with PD (Arendt et al., 1983), >20% of the neuronal DEG that have an orthologous gene in the fly are also found among the most deregulated genes across PD fly models.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and statistical analysis of the overlap.

claim: Of the 2486 significantly differentially expressed human genes, 1149 have a fly orthologue, and of these, 28.46% overlap with the deregulated fly genes.
source: This is highly significant: of the 2486 significantly differentially expressed human genes, 1149 have a fly orthologue, and of these, 28.46% overlap with the deregulated fly genes (5% top and bottom genes listed in Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers and percentages of overlapping genes.

claim: The overlap between human and fly differentially expressed genes is statistically significant (p = 9.06e-76).
source: Performing a hypergeometric test confirms that this overlap is significant (p, 9.06e-76).
evidence: A hypergeometric test was performed to assess statistical significance.

claim: Gene ontology analysis shows that processes most strikingly enriched in both fly models and human NBM are those related to synaptic function.
source: Markedly, this shows that the processes most strikingly enriched in both fly models and human NBM are those related to synaptic function (Figure 3b).
evidence: Gene ontology enrichment is shown in Figure 3b.

claim: More than half of the differentially expressed genes found in human and flies are present in the synapse-specific portal SynGo.
source: Indeed, more than half of the DEG found in human and flies are present in the synapse-specific portal SynGo (Koopmans et al., 2019; Figure 3a; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The overlap with SynGo is shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Enrichment was found for presynaptic function, including synaptic exocytosis, axon guidance, synapse organization, ion transport, and protein homeostasis.
source: We found enrichment for presynaptic function, including synaptic exocytosis, axon guidance, synapse organization, ion transport, and protein homeostasis (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: Enriched processes are shown in Figures 3b and c.

claim: Enrichment of genes involved in RNA regulation and mitochondrial function was also found.
source: Additionally, we also found enrichment of genes involved in RNA regulation and mitochondrial function that are also important for the functioning of synaptic terminals (Supplementary file 7; Gorenberg and Chandra, 2017; Morais et al., 2009; Snead and Eliezer, 2019; Uytterhoeven et al., 2011; Verstreken et al., 2005).
evidence: The enrichment is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Comparing the vulnerable gene signatures from each of the PD fly models to the DEGs from the human samples does not show any greater similarity between the LRRK2 mutants compared to the other PD mutants.
source: Of note, while the human samples all have LRRK2 variant mutations, comparing the vulnerable gene signatures from each of the PD fly models to the DEGs from the human samples does not show any greater similarity between the LRRK2 mutants compared to the other PD mutants (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this comparison result.

claim: Cholinergic olfactory neurons of young familial fly PD models and human PD patients both show preferential transcriptional deregulation of genes that regulate synaptic function.
source: In summary, cholinergic olfactory neurons of young familial fly PD models and human PD patients both show preferential transcriptional deregulation of genes that regulate synaptic function.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of fly and human data.

claim: The five PD mutant knock-ins show significantly weaker Ca2+-responses at OPN synapses compared to controls.
source: In contrast, the five PD mutant knock-ins show significantly weaker Ca2+-responses (e.g. hLRRK2G2019S in Figure 4c and d, pink points, and quantified in Figure 4g, middle bar; 'OPN>wt CDS -').
evidence: Ca2+ responses were measured using GCaMP3 imaging and quantified in Figure 4g.

claim: PD mutants expressing wild-type PD genes using GH146-Gal4 show synaptic Ca2+ signals similar to controls.
source: PD mutants expressing wild-type PD genes using GH146-Gal4 show synaptic Ca2+ signals similar to controls, indicating the PD genes are required in OPN of these young animals to maintain robust synaptic function (Figure 4g, right bar; 'OPN>wt CDS +').
evidence: Rescue of Ca2+ signals is shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The hLRRK2G2029S knock-in flies are not rescued by OPN-specific expression of hLRRK2.
source: Note that while hLRRK2 wild-type knock-in flies are very similar to wild-type controls (Figure 4g, right bar), the hLRRK2G2029S knock-in flies are not rescued by OPN-specific expression of hLRRK2 (Figure 4g, right bar; 'OPN >wt CDS +').
evidence: The lack of rescue is shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The G2019S mutation in LRRK2 is dominant.
source: This is in agreement with the G2019S mutation being dominant (West et al., 2005; Zimprich et al., 2004).
evidence: The dominant nature of the mutation is supported by citations to West et al., 2005 and Zimprich et al., 2004.

claim: PD mutants have a significantly larger synaptic area in the calyx compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, the PD mutants have a significantly larger area compared to controls, despite very similar GFP expression levels (Figure 4e, f and h).
evidence: Synaptic area measurements are shown in Figures 4e, f, and h.

claim: The synaptic area defect in PD mutants is cell-autonomous and rescued by OPN-selective expression of the wild-type CDS, except for LRRK2G2019S.
source: Again, this defect is cell-autonomous, because it is rescued by OPN-selective expression of the wild-type CDS, except - again - for LRRK2G2019S agreeing with it being a dominant mutant (Figure 4h).
evidence: Rescue of synaptic area is shown in Figure 4h.

claim: OPN of young PD mutants display cell-autonomous presynaptic defects: even though the synaptic area is increased, synaptic Ca2+ signals are diminished.
source: Thus, OPN of young PD mutants display cell-autonomous presynaptic defects: even though the synaptic area is increased, synaptic Ca2+ signals are diminished.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the Ca2+ imaging and synaptic area measurements.

claim: Young PD mutants (5 days old) do not show SING defects.
source: While old (25 days) PD mutants show PAM-dependent locomotion dysfunction in the SING assay (Figure 1b, SING old), young (5 days) PD mutants do not show SING defects (Figure 1b, SING young).
evidence: SING performance is shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Young PD mutants have functional PAM neurons.
source: While old (25 days) PD mutants show PAM-dependent locomotion dysfunction in the SING assay (Figure 1b, SING old), young (5 days) PD mutants do not show SING defects (Figure 1b, SING young). These data indicate PAM neurons are functional in young PD mutants.
evidence: The functionality of PAM neurons is inferred from the absence of SING defects in young mutants.

claim: Control and wild-type knock-in flies show a robust odor preference in two odor tests.
source: Control and wild-type knock-in flies show a robust odor preference in these two odor tests (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Odor preference is shown in Figures 5a and b.

claim: Knock-in flies carrying pathogenic mutations behave indecisive in odor preference tests.
source: Conversely, the knock-in flies carrying the pathogenic mutations behave indecisive (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Indecisive behavior is shown in Figures 5a and b.

claim: Young PD mutants show olfactory behavior defects.
source: Hence, young PD mutants show olfactory behavior defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the odor preference test results.

claim: Expressing the relevant wild-type CDS selectively in the OPN of pathogenic knock-in mutant flies restores olfactory performance back to control levels.
source: This manipulation restores olfactory performance back to control levels (Figure 5c and d; 'OPN>wt CDS +', green label) when compared to PD mutants lacking OPN expression (Figure 5c and d; '-').
evidence: Rescue of olfactory performance is shown in Figures 5c and d.

claim: The LRRK2G2019S mutant remains unaffected by OPN-specific expression of wild-type LRRK2, consistent with its classification as a dominant mutant.
source: However, the LRRK2G2019S mutant remains unaffected, consistent with its classification as a dominant mutant.
evidence: The lack of rescue in LRRK2G2019S mutants is consistent with the dominant nature of the mutation.

claim: lrrkKO flies show an olfactory performance defect.
source: Note that lrrkKO flies also show an olfactory performance defect (Figure 5c and d; '-') and that expressing hLRRK2 cDNA specifically in the OPN of lrrkKO rescues this defect (Figure 5c and d; 'OPN>hLRRK2 +', green label).
evidence: Olfactory performance defect and rescue are shown in Figures 5c and d.

claim: hLRRK2 is a functional protein that can compensate for the function of the fly orthologue in the context of olfactory performance.
source: This indicates hLRRK2 is a functional protein that, in this context, can compensate for the function of the fly orthologue.
evidence: The rescue of lrrkKO by hLRRK2 expression indicates functional compensation.

claim: Expressing wild-type CDS in T1-interneurons of the visual system does not improve olfactory performance in PD mutants.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that the rescue of the olfactory performance in PD mutants is specific for OPN, because expressing wild-type CDS in another affected cell type, 'T1-interneurons of the visual system', of knock-in PD animals (we chose to test this in Rab39BG192R mutants) does not improve olfactory performance (Figure 5c and d; 'T1>hRab39B +', red label).
evidence: The lack of rescue by T1-specific expression is shown in Figures 5c and d.

claim: A cell-autonomous defect in cholinergic OPN causes olfactory defects across PD mutants.
source: Hence, a cell-autonomous defect in cholinergic OPN causes olfactory defects across PD mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell-type-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Young PD mutants (aux, synj, and LRRK2) have olfactory defects while displaying normal DAN function (SING).
source: Our data indicates that young PD mutants (aux, synj, and LRRK2) have olfactory defects while displaying normal DAN function (SING).
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral phenotypes observed in young mutants.

claim: Aged auxR927G, synjR258Q, and hLRRK2G2019S knock-in animals exhibit both olfactory preference defects and progressive DAN (SING) dysfunction.
source: Conversely, aged auxR927G, synjR258Q, and hLRRK2G2019S knock-in animals exhibit both olfactory preference defects and progressive DAN (SING) dysfunction (Figure 6a; line graphs; 'DAN-dependent movement behavior').
evidence: Behavioral defects in aged mutants are shown in Figure 6a.

claim: All three 25-day-old knock-in mutants show a significant reduction in DAN afferent innervation area onto mushroom bodies.
source: In line with the SING behavioral defect, all three 25-day-old knock-in mutants show a significant reduction in DAN afferent (Figure 6a, left bar; 'OPN>wt CDS -'; 'DAN synapse morphology').
evidence: DAN synapse morphology is shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Expressing the wild-type PD gene in OPN of auxR927G and synjR258Q mutants using GH146-Gal4 rescues the DAN-associated SING and synaptic connectivity defects in old PD mutants.
source: We find these genetic manipulations rescue the DAN-associated SING and synaptic connectivity defects in old PD mutants (Figure 6a).
evidence: Rescue of DAN defects is shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Expressing endoAS75D in OPN of hLRRK2G2019S mutants rescues the DAN-associated SING and synaptic connectivity defects in old PD mutants.
source: Given that hLRRK2G2019S is dominant, we did not express the wild-type hLRRK2 in OPN, but endoAS75D that we showed previously genetically interacts with lrrk (Matta et al., 2012; Figure 6a, right bar; 'OPN>endoAS75D +'; 'DAN synapse morphology'). We find these genetic manipulations rescue the DAN-associated SING and synaptic connectivity defects in old PD mutants (Figure 6a).
evidence: Rescue by endoAS75D expression is shown in Figure 6a, supported by citation to Matta et al., 2012.

claim: Functional OPN have a cell-nonautonomous effect to prevent DAN dysfunction that emerges at old age in the PD mutants.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that functional OPN have a cell-nonautonomous effect to prevent DAN dysfunction that emerges at old age in the PD mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments showing OPN function affects DAN health.

claim: Feeding nicotine to hLRRK2G20190S mutants does not rescue the olfactory preference defect.
source: While feeding nicotine does not rescue the olfactory preference defect of hLRRK2G2019S mutants, it also does not rescue the OPN synapse morphology defect or the OPN-associated defects in synaptic Ca-imaging (Figure 6b).
evidence: The lack of rescue by nicotine is shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Nicotine rescues the DAN-associated defects in hLRRK2G2019S mutants, including SING, synapse loss and defects in Ca-imaging at DAN synapses.
source: Interestingly, nicotine does rescue the DAN-associated defects, including SING, synapse loss and defects in Ca-imaging at DAN synapses (Figure 6c).
evidence: Rescue of DAN defects by nicotine is shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The results are consistent with the role of OPN function, specifically acetylcholine release, in preventing DAN damage in PD mutants.
source: These results are consistent with the role of OPN function, specifically acetylcholine release, in preventing DAN damage in PD mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nicotine treatment experiments.

claim: Human induced neurons were generated from iPSC in which an LRRK2G2019S mutation was engineered.
source: We therefore generated human induced neurons derived from iPSC in which we engineered an LRRK2G2019S mutation and differentiated the cells into DAN (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Kriks et al., 2011; Nolbrant et al., 2017).
evidence: The generation of iPSC-derived neurons is described and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The differentiation protocol results in >50% DAN in both the LRRK2G2019S mutant line and the isogenic control.
source: Our protocol results in >50% DAN in both the LRRK2G2019S mutant line and the isogenic control (Figure 6d, Figure 6—figure supplement 1e and f).
evidence: DAN differentiation efficiency is shown in Figure 6d and Figure 6—figure supplement 1e and f.

claim: LRRK2G2019S mutant DAN are significantly less active and the amplitudes of their Ca2+-spikes are smaller than those in isogenic controls.
source: To assess neuronal activity, we expressed GCaMP6f and find that LRRK2G2019S mutant DAN are significantly less active and the amplitudes of their Ca2+-spikes are smaller than those in isogenic controls (Figure 6e).
evidence: Neuronal activity was measured using GCaMP6f and shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Incubating differentiated DAN with nicotine rescues the LRRK2G2019S-induced neuronal activity defects.
source: Next, we incubated the differentiated DAN with nicotine and found this rescues the LRRK2G2019S-induced neuronal activity defects.
evidence: The rescue by nicotine is described in the text.

claim: No rescue was observed when cells were co-incubated with mecamylamine, a non-competitive antagonist of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: This effect is specific to nicotine as no rescue was observed when cells were co-incubated with mecamylamine, a non-competitive antagonist of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, trumping the effects of nicotine (Figure 6e).
evidence: The specificity of nicotine's effect is shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The positive effect of nicotine on PD mutants is conserved between flies and iPSC-derived DAN.
source: Hence, the positive effect of nicotine on PD mutants is conserved between flies and iPSC-derived DAN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nicotine treatment experiments in both flies and human cells.

claim: Parkinsonism is currently diagnosed based on motor defects that only occur following significant DAN degeneration.
source: Parkinsonism is currently diagnosed based on motor defects that only occur following significant DAN degeneration.
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice.

claim: Patients suffer from non-motoric problems decades earlier, including sleep problems and hyposmia.
source: However, patients suffer from non-motoric problems decades earlier, including sleep problems and hyposmia (the inability to properly discern odors) (Yamakado and Takahashi, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yamakado and Takahashi, 2024.

claim: Most non-motoric problems in PD are not responsive to dopamine replacement therapy, suggesting other transmitter systems are involved.
source: Most of these non-motoric problems are not responsive to dopamine replacement therapy, suggesting other transmitter systems are involved.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical observations.

claim: Cholinergic system failure is one of the earliest defects across five different Parkinsonism fly models.
source: Using unbiased methodology, we find cholinergic system failure as one of the earliest defects across five different Parkinsonism fly models and we show that synaptic failure of specific cholinergic projection neurons (OPN) causes non-motor problems, including hyposmia.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Synaptic failure of specific cholinergic projection neurons (OPN) causes non-motor problems, including hyposmia.
source: Using unbiased methodology, we find cholinergic system failure as one of the earliest defects across five different Parkinsonism fly models and we show that synaptic failure of specific cholinergic projection neurons (OPN) causes non-motor problems, including hyposmia.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Cholinergic defects in several brain regions have been observed in patients, including the olfactory bulb and the occipital cortex.
source: Also in patients, cholinergic defects in several brain regions have been observed, including the olfactory bulb and the occipital cortex (Kuhl et al., 1996; Shimada et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuhl et al., 1996 and Shimada et al., 2009.

claim: Cholinergic defects correlate with several non-motor symptoms, including impaired olfactory and visual processing.
source: These defects correlate with several non-motor symptoms, including impaired olfactory and visual processing (Bohnen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bohnen et al., 2010.

claim: Cholinergic failure occurs ahead of dopaminergic system failure in flies.
source: We now place cholinergic failure firmly ahead of dopaminergic system failure in flies, and we suggest that dysfunction of specific cholinergic projection neurons may be a prodromal signal of disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal sequence of defects observed in the study.

claim: Dysfunction of specific cholinergic projection neurons may be a prodromal signal of disease.
source: We now place cholinergic failure firmly ahead of dopaminergic system failure in flies, and we suggest that dysfunction of specific cholinergic projection neurons may be a prodromal signal of disease.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the findings of the study.

claim: DAN have a high density of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: However, DAN have a high density of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and evidence suggests that stimulating these receptors enhances DAN survival (Brimblecombe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brimblecombe et al., 2018.

claim: Stimulating nicotinic acetylcholine receptors enhances DAN survival.
source: However, DAN have a high density of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and evidence suggests that stimulating these receptors enhances DAN survival (Brimblecombe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brimblecombe et al., 2018.

claim: Epidemiological data indicates that nicotine exposure from chronic smoking protects against PD.
source: This is supported by epidemiological data indicating that nicotine exposure from chronic smoking protects against PD (Janssens et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019), and various studies, including the work we present here, show that direct nicotine supplementation mitigates DAN dysfunction in mouse and fly PD models (Chambers et al., 2013; Fares et al., 2023; Olsen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janssens et al., 2022 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Direct nicotine supplementation mitigates DAN dysfunction in mouse and fly PD models.
source: This is supported by epidemiological data indicating that nicotine exposure from chronic smoking protects against PD (Janssens et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019), and various studies, including the work we present here, show that direct nicotine supplementation mitigates DAN dysfunction in mouse and fly PD models (Chambers et al., 2013; Fares et al., 2023; Olsen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2013; Fares et al., 2023; Olsen et al., 2023, and data from the current study.

claim: Factors affecting the function of OPN or cholinergic neurons might lead to DAN problems and degeneration by absence of insufficient innervation or activity.
source: These findings imply that factors affecting the function of OPN or cholinergic neurons might, by absence of insufficient innervation or activity, lead to DAN problems and degeneration, warranting further exploration of the underlying molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The findings reveal a common trigger relevant for both familial and idiopathic cases of PD.
source: Our findings reveal a common trigger relevant for both familial and idiopathic cases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of fly models and human patient samples.

claim: Observations of Lewy body pathology in postmortem samples suggest the disease may nucleate at specific sites and then propagate.
source: Observations of Lewy body pathology in postmortem samples suggest the disease may nucleate at specific sites and then propagate.
evidence: This is a statement about observations in the field.

claim: Early aggregation of α-Synuclein occurs in the olfactory bulb.
source: This includes spreading of the disease between the gut and the brain as well as early aggregation of α-Synuclein, a synaptic protein, in the olfactory bulb (Braak et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Braak et al., 2003a.

claim: The presence of protein aggregates in the gut and olfactory bulb is consistent with protein homeostasis and synaptic defects that ultimately contribute to the aggregation of α-Synuclein.
source: The presence of protein aggregates in these areas is consistent with protein homeostasis and synaptic defects that ultimately contribute to the aggregation of α-Synuclein (Chu et al., 2009; Friedman et al., 2012; Sarkar et al., 2007; Webb et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chu et al., 2009; Friedman et al., 2012; Sarkar et al., 2007; Webb et al., 2003.

claim: In idiopathic disease, the gut and olfactory bulb synapses are more easily exposed to environmental toxins that cause protein misfolding and aggregation.
source: In idiopathic disease, there is some evidence this is because the gut and olfactory bulb synapses are more easily exposed to environmental toxins that cause protein misfolding and aggregation (Braak et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Braak et al., 2003b.

claim: Single-cell sequencing shows the deregulation of several synaptic pathways in the PD knock-in mutants.
source: However, different mechanisms may be at play since our single-cell sequencing shows the deregulation of several synaptic pathways in the PD knock-in mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single-cell sequencing data.

claim: Several genes mutated in familial forms of PD have proposed synaptic functions.
source: While several genes mutated in familial forms of PD have proposed synaptic functions (endocytosis, synaptic autophagy, etc.), others may be affecting the synapse indirectly (e.g. mitochondria, transport, etc.).
evidence: This is a statement about the known functions of PD genes.

claim: Some PD genes may be affecting the synapse indirectly through effects on mitochondria, transport, etc.
source: While several genes mutated in familial forms of PD have proposed synaptic functions (endocytosis, synaptic autophagy, etc.), others may be affecting the synapse indirectly (e.g. mitochondria, transport, etc.).
evidence: This is a speculation about how different PD genes might affect synapses.

claim: The GH146-Gal4 line drives expression in OPNs (that are cholinergic) and one pair of inhibitory APL neurons (that are GABAergic).
